Chapter Three: The Importance of Honest Self-Examination
Now that you’ve got a handle on personal responsibility and how behavioral loops work, let’s talk about the next big step—honest self-examination.
Think of self-examination like holding up a mirror. Not just to your appearance, but to your motives, your fears, and what you really want. It takes real courage to see yourself clearly, without any filters or excuses. It can be tough—most of us would rather not admit where we’ve slipped up or face those parts of ourselves we're not so proud of. But here’s the thing: if you skip this step, real change just doesn’t happen.
Picture a navigator plotting a journey. If you want to get where you’re going, you have to know exactly where you’re starting. If you guess, or pretend you’re already somewhere else, you just get lost. Honest self-examination works the same way—it gives you a clear map of where you are right now, so you can figure out the best way forward.
There are a few key parts to doing this well.
First, be willing to see both your strengths and your weaknesses. Don’t shy away from either.
Second, be open to feedback—even the kind that stings a bit—from people you trust. Sometimes, that outside perspective shows you things you’d never spot on your own.
And third, try to see your patterns as they really are, not just how you wish they were.
Want a practical way to start? Try keeping a journal. Write down moments from your day that really got a reaction out of you—maybe frustration, maybe excitement. After a while, you’ll start to notice patterns.
For instance, you might see that you feel ignored at work, but then realize you usually hold back from sharing your ideas. Spotting that pattern is the first step to changing it.
Another useful tool? Ask a friend or a colleague you trust for honest feedback. Sure, it might feel awkward at first, but sometimes the things we can’t see about ourselves are crystal clear to others—and their insights can make all the difference.
Here’s something to watch out for: mixing up your intentions with your actions. It’s easy to judge ourselves by what we meant to do, but others see what we actually do. For real growth, you want your actions to line up with your values—not just your good intentions.
And remember, self-examination isn’t about beating yourself up or dwelling on the past. It’s about learning and moving forward. When you face your reality honestly, but with a bit of compassion, you give yourself the chance to make choices that fit what really matters to you.
